title: Palm Nut Soup
author: Mirlene Owusu
desc: Built on tinned palm nut cream — and the cue is exact: the soup is done when you no longer see foam on top and the oil is visible.
longDesc: Abenkwan is the richest soup in Ghana and Osseo-Asare says it surpasses all others for colour, flavour and texture. This version uses tinned palm nut cream rather than pounding fresh palm fruit, which is what most cooks outside Ghana actually do. Beef neck bones and smoked fish simmer an hour and a half to two hours with garlic, ginger, scotch bonnet, tomato paste and bay. The palm cream is strained with six and a half cups of water, blended vegetables go in and cook half-covered fifteen minutes, the meats return, and it simmers thirty to forty-five minutes more.
ingredients: 1 tin (1 lb 10 oz) palm nut cream
steps: Simmer the beef neck bones and smoked fish with the garlic, ginger, scotch bonnet, tomato paste, bay leaves, seasoning and vegetable oil for 1 1/2 to 2 hours.
Strain the palm nut cream with the 6 1/2 cups of water into a clean pot.
Blend the onion, tomatoes, red bell pepper and ginger.
Add the blended vegetables to the palm liquid and cook half-covered 15 minutes.
Add the cooked meats and fish.
The soup is done when you no longer see foam on top and the oil is visible on top.
Serve with fufu (GHA001) or omo tuo (GHA003).
chefTips: The doneness cue is the best-written one in the Ghanaian soup literature: no foam on top, oil visible on top. Both conditions, not one.
Half-covered for the fifteen-minute vegetable stage. Fully covered and it will not reduce; uncovered and it spits palm oil across the kitchen.
Strain the palm cream with the water rather than stirring it in. The fibre that comes out of a tin is not pleasant in the finished soup.
An hour and a half to two hours on the neck bones. They are the whole point of the dish — collagen-heavy and cheap — and they will not give up their body in less.
Smoked fish goes in with the meat from the start, not at the end. It is a seasoning here as much as a protein.
Osseo-Asare's description is the best thing written about this soup: it surpasses all other soups for richness, colour, flavour and texture.

Every documented palm nut soup starts from a different base — fresh pounded nuts, tinned cream, a concentrate, or straight palm oil. They are genuinely different soups and the sources do not agree on which is correct.
commonMistakes: Stirring the tinned cream in without straining.
Fully covering the pot during the vegetable stage.
Serving while foam is still on the surface.
Adding the smoked fish at the end.
sources: Adapted from 'Ghanaian Palm Nut Soup', savorythoughts.com, byline as printed 'By Mirlene', 2 June 2026. Yield as printed: 6 servings. SINGLE-PASS on the quantities — this page was read once and the figures are therefore UNVERIFIED against a second fetch. FLAGS: the site is a branded-seasoning blog, its listed owners are 'AJ & Mirlene', and no Ghanaian background for the authors could be confirmed. One ingredient is the site's own branded product ('Savory Thoughts all-purpose seasoning'), rendered above as a generic all-purpose seasoning.

Ingredients exactly as printed. Meat group: 2 lbs. beef neck bones; 3 pieces smoked fish; Beef tripe (optional); 6 garlic cloves; 4 tbsp. Savory Thoughts all-purpose seasoning; 2 thumb-size pieces ginger; 1 habanero or scotch bonnet; 4 tbsp. tomato paste; 3 bay leaves; ¼ cup vegetable oil. Soup group: 1 can (1 lb. 10 oz.) palm nut cream (Adepa brand recommended); 6½ cups water; ½ cup vegetable oil; 1 large onion; 4 large tomatoes; ½ red bell pepper; thumb-size ginger.
Method as printed: simmer the meat 1½-2 hours; strain the palm cream with the water; add the blended vegetables, cook half-covered 15 minutes, add the meats, and simmer 30-45 minutes.

THE DONENESS CUE, verbatim, and the reason this version carries the main entry despite the single-pass caveat: 'The soup is done when you no longer see foam on top, and the oil is visible on top.' That is a precise two-part observable endpoint and no other palm nut soup source gives one as clear.

CONTEXT, from Fran Osseo-Asare, Gastronomica, Winter 2002, byline 'By Fran Osseo-Asare': 'Abenkwan is made with the small red fruits of the palm tree, called palmnuts, and includes the strained pulp and oil from the fruit surrounding the palm kernels.' And it 'surpasses all other soups' for 'richness, color, flavor, and texture.'

THE FOUR DOCUMENTED BASES, all different and NOT reconciled. (1) Pulp extracted from 1200 g of boiled fresh nuts, with a 25-minute boil of 3000 ml of juice — the KNUST standardised study below. (2) Tinned palm nut cream, here. (3) A commercial concentrate, 'EZ Palmnut' — see GHA021. (4) Two cups of straight palm oil with no palm fruit at all — see GHA020, where that source's internal contradiction is set out. Endpoints differ too: 'oil accumulates' (KNUST), 'no foam, oil visible' (here), 'somewhat thickened' (GHA020).

FOR COMPARISON ONLY, not published as a recipe: Appiah CA et al., African Journal of Food, Agriculture, Nutrition & Development 20(3):15898-15918, 2020 (KNUST) gives a lab-standardised abenkwan of 1200 g African oil palm nut, 20 g salt, 7 g powdered pepper, 265 g onion, 317 g fresh tomatoes, plus 135 g smoked catfish and 38 g herrings in its variant. Method verbatim: 'Palm nuts of 1200 g was washed and boiled with 2000 ml of water until the nuts were soft. The palm nut was sieved out and pounded until the flesh was peeled off. The pounded nuts were dissolved in 2500 ml of warm water.' Then 'The palm pulp juice of 3000 ml was added and allowed to boil for 25 minutes.' QUANTITY ANOMALY IN THAT PAPER, recorded and NOT corrected: the nuts are dissolved in 2500 ml of warm water but 3000 ml of palm pulp juice is then added, and the 500 ml difference is unexplained. Whether it is a misprint is not known.
The Ghana Cookbook (Osseo-Asare & Baëta, Hippocrene 2015) has a 'Palm Nut Soup (Abε Nkwan)' at 10 to 12 servings, but its quantities were not obtainable behind the publisher's paywall.
storage: 4 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen. The palm oil sets solid when cold.
reheating: Simmer gently until the oil re-melts and rises.
healthBenefits: Palm fruit pulp is exceptionally rich in provitamin-A carotenoids and vitamin E tocotrienols.
Neck bones yield collagen, glycine and minerals.
Smoked fish adds protein, iodine and omega-3 fats.
High in lycopene from the long-cooked tomato.
culturalNote: Abenkwan is the soup people travel for, and the version made from fresh pounded palm fruit is a different and better thing than any tin — which is precisely why the tinned version exists and is used everywhere outside Ghana. The foam-and-oil cue is the same whichever base you start from, because what it is really telling you is that the palm has cooked out.
